claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has a single-phase BCC structure.
The baseline alloy has high density.
The baseline alloy has insufficient room-temperature ductility and exhibits brittle failure.
A minor Si addition will induce secondary intermetallic precipitation in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The Si-induced secondary phase may be a Laves phase or silicide such as (Hf,Zr)Si2.
The secondary intermetallic phase will form a continuous or semi-continuous reticulated network along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
A suitable Si concentration can trigger secondary-phase precipitation without disrupting continuity of the primary BCC matrix.
The reticulated intermetallic network will obstruct crack propagation.
The network will force cracks to deflect, branch, or arrest.
Crack deflection, branching, or arrest will increase fracture toughness and room-temperature ductility.
The secondary precipitates will provide precipitation hardening.
The Si-added alloy will have greater room-temperature compressive plastic strain than the baseline.
The Si-added alloy will have greater room-temperature compressive yield strength than the baseline.
The Si addition will increase alloy density by less than 2%.
The predicted marginal density change is attributed to Si having low atomic mass relative to Hf and Zr.
Above an unspecified Si-concentration threshold, a fully brittle continuous intermetallic skeleton may form and embrittle the alloy.
The proposed strength-ductility benefit is restricted to room-temperature uniaxial compression.
Phase identification and fracture-surface analysis can distinguish the proposed phase-network mechanism from solid-solution hardening.
